world.title: KENYA: Auxiliary Bishop of Kenya’s Nairobi Archdiocese, Ordained in Solemn Eucharistic Celebration
world.description:
By Rose Achiego Ande
Kenya’s Catholic Archdiocese of Nairobi was filled with joy, prayer, and thanksgiving as Rt. Rev. Obed Muriungi Karobia was ordained Auxiliary Bishop in a solemn Eucharistic celebration held at the Holy Family Minor Basilica on Wednesday, May 6, bringing together bishops, priests, religious men and women, government leaders, family members, and thousands of faithful from across Kenya and beyond.
The sacred liturgy reflected the beauty and richness of the Catholic Church’s apostolic tradition as the faithful gathered to witness the conferral of the fullness of the Sacrament of Holy Orders upon Bishop Karobia, who now joins the episcopal ministry in service to the people of God in Nairobi.
Presiding over the celebration, the Apostolic Nuncio to Kenya, Archbishop Bert van Megen, delivered a deeply reflective homily centered on the biblical meaning of the name “Obed,” which signifies servant.
Addressing the bishop-elect just before the ordinatio, Archbishop Van Megen warmly welcomed him into the family of the Archdiocese of Nairobi, drawing parallels between Bishop Karobia and the biblical Obed, son of Ruth, whose story is recounted in Sacred Scripture.
“You have come from afar, coming from Meru diocese, almost like an adopted son, much like the biblical Obed, who himself was born of a foreign mother, Ruth,” the Apostolic Nuncio said.
He described the Holy Family Basilica as a new Bethlehem — the “House of Bread”  where Christ continues to nourish His people through the Eucharist. Reflecting on the story of Ruth and Naomi, the Nuncio emphasized fidelity, humility, and service as the foundation of authentic Christian leadership. “Service is the deepest vocation of anyone who truly wishes to follow the Lord,” Archbishop Van Megen said.
Drawing from the Gospel of the washing of the feet during the Last Supper, the Apostolic Nuncio reminded the faithful that episcopal ministry is rooted in humble service after the example of Christ, who knelt before His disciples.
[caption id=attachment_24618 align=alignright width=300] A section of congregants during Mass[/caption]
“The readings of today all speak about servants, about Jesus who kneels to wash the feet of His disciples,” he reflected, calling upon the bishop-elect to remain close to the poor, the suffering, and all entrusted to his pastoral care.
In his welcoming remarks, Archbishop Philip Anyolo expressed gratitude to God for the appointment of Bishop Karobia, noting that the Archdiocese of Nairobi continues to experience growing pastoral needs that require additional assistance in episcopal ministry.
“The increasing pastoral demands of the Archdiocese continue to require additional assistance in the episcopal ministry in accordance with the Church’s solicitude for the care of souls,” Archbishop Anyolo said.
He assured the new Auxiliary Bishop of the prayers and support of the clergy, religious, and lay faithful as he begins his ministry within the Metropolitan See of Nairobi.
In his address, the Chairman of the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB) and Archbishop of the Catholic Archdiocese of Kisumu, Maurice Muhatia, described the ordination as both a celebration and a profound profession of faith in the continuity of the apostolic mission of the Church.
“We are united with the Church of ancient times, united with the Apostles themselves in the Upper Room contemplating the Lord,” Archbishop Muhatia said.
He emphasized that through the ordination of bishops, the Church remains firmly linked to Christ through apostolic succession handed down across generations. “The Holy Father, in a very special way, is confirming us in the faith and assuring us of our link to the Apostles and to Christ Himself,” he added.
Archbishop Muhatia further welcomed Bishop Karobia into the fraternity of the bishops of Kenya on behalf of members of KCCB, assuring him of brotherhood, unity, and collaboration in the mission of the Church.
“We welcome you to the Conference of Bishops of Kenya and invite you to feel at home in the midst of brothers. We are now henceforth your brothers, and you will be our brother,” he said.
The KCCB Chairman also formally presented Bishop Karobia with key documents of the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, including the Conference statutes, bylaws, and strategic framework that guide the pastoral and administrative mission of the Church in Kenya.
A deeply symbolic moment during the ordination was the reading of the Apostolic Bull from the Holy Father, officially confirming the appointment of Bishop Karobia as Auxiliary Bishop of Nairobi. The reading signified communion between the local Church and the universal Church under the leadership of the Successor of Peter.
The congregation was also drawn into profound prayer during the Litany of Saints, when the bishop-elect lay prostrate before the altar in complete surrender to God’s will as the Church invoked the intercession of the saints.
The laying on of hands by the bishops and the Prayer of Ordination followed, signifying the continuity of apostolic succession handed down from the Apostles through the ages. Bishop Karobia was then anointed with Sacred Chrism and presented with the Book of the Gospels, the episcopal ring, mitre, and crosier — sacred symbols of his ministry to teach, sanctify, and shepherd the flock entrusted to his care.
In his remarks, Rt. Rev. Obed Karobia expressed gratitude to God, the Holy Father, bishops, priests, religious, family members, and all the faithful who have accompanied him throughout his vocation journey. He called for continued prayers as he embraces the mission of serving God’s people with humility, fidelity, and pastoral charity.
The ordination marked not merely the elevation of a new bishop, but a renewed invitation to the Church to embrace servant leadership rooted in Christ, the Good Shepherd, who came not to be served, but to serve.

world.title: KENYA: ‘Seeds of Energy’ Solar Initiative, Launched in Mathari, Nyeri
world.description:
Fr. Michael Maurice
The Archdiocese of Nyeri on Tuesday, April 28, commissioned the Seeds of Energy Solar Project at Mathari in a colorful ceremony attended by distinguished guests.
In his remarks, Archbishop Anthony Muheria of Nyeri Archdiocese noted that the project is a significant step in addressing climate change, in line with the vision of Laudato Si by Pope Francis. He emphasized that the initiative reflects a holistic and sustainable approach, supported by partnerships that promote environmental stewardship.
He further highlighted the role of solar energy in supporting processes such as the production of hydrogen and oxygen.
Bishop Peter Kimani Ndung’u of Kenya’s Embu Diocese commended the Archdiocese of Nyeri for the initiative, highlighting the importance of renewable energy in safeguarding the environment and promoting the well-being of future generations.
Governor Mutahi Kahiga praised the project as a bold step towards a greener, cleaner, and brighter future.
The Chief Guest, H.E. Zainab Hawa Bangura, described the project as a reflection of visionary leadership and responsible stewardship, emphasizing that sustainability is a moral responsibility. She lauded the initiative as a model of what can be achieved through faith, planning, and collaboration, noting its potential to support growth in education, healthcare, and environmental conservation.
A landmark initiative positioning the Archdiocese of Nyeri as a leader in sustainable development and care for creation.

world.title: UGANDA: Bishop Calls on Christians to Reject Modern Idols and Put God First for Peace
world.description:
Fr. Isaac Ojok
The Bishop of Arua diocese in North Western Uganda, Rt. Rev. Sabino Ochan Odoki, has called on Christians to reject modern-day idols and embrace God as the foundation for lasting peace in society.
Bishop Odoki made the appeal during the closing Eucharistic celebration of the provincial Prayer and peace Week held at Lango College, in Lira diocese where he presided over the final Mass commissioning peace pilgrims to return to their respective dioceses as ambassadors of peace.
The Prayer Peace Week has been taking place in Lira diocese under the theme, “Peace Be With You” drawn from John 20:19. The week-long pastoral and spiritual gathering attracted participants from the four dioceses under the Gulu Ecclesiastical Province, namely Gulu Archdiocese, Lira diocese, Nebbi catholic diocese, and Arua diocese including Kotido in North Eastern Uganda.
In his homily, Bishop Odoki warned that many people today have allowed worldly distractions to take the place of God in their lives, something he said continues to deprive society of genuine peace.
“Idols take away our minds from the true God. God becomes secondary while other things take priority in our lives,” the bishop said.
He listed money, wealth, political and economic power, social media, artificial intelligence, prestige, excessive pursuit of comfort, alcohol abuse, and obsession with physical appearance as some of the modern idols affecting society today.
The bishop particularly criticized the growing tendency among some people to prioritize outward appearance over spiritual values.
“People are changing their color, spending resources on appearances and forgetting God,” he said, adding that even within the Church, the struggle for positions and authority can become an idol when people seek offices for personal glory instead of service.
Bishop Odoki noted that peace can only flourish where people put God first and live according to the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit.
“The gift of the Holy Spirit should help us to promote peace. If peace is becoming a challenge, then it means we are not putting the fruits of the Holy Spirit into practice,” he said.
The bishop explained that the Eucharistic celebration marked the commissioning of peace pilgrims to go out as messengers of peace to the world. He said the Mass of the Holy Spirit was intentionally chosen so that the Spirit of God may accompany the mission of peace entrusted to all participants.
Reflecting on the state of the country, Bishop Odoki observed that many people lack inner peace and are living with growing discontent.
“We need to understand peace as a gift from God which we must carry back home to our dioceses and communities,” he emphasized.
He reminded Christians that at creation God breathed His Spirit into humanity and that through Baptism believers receive the Holy Spirit whose gifts bear fruits such as charity, peace, patience, kindness, self-control, modesty, and chastity.
The bishop also encouraged Ugandans to promote dialogue, respect human rights, uphold democratic values, and reject violence in order to build peaceful communities.
He further urged Christians to fight corruption, tribalism, favoritism, laziness, and poverty, saying such vices continue to undermine harmony and development in society.
Citing the Gospel reading of the day, Bishop Odoki said Jesus commands believers to love one another, noting that love remains the foundation of every peaceful society.
Quoting the theological virtues of faith, hope, and love as taught by St Paul, the Bishop stressed that love is the greatest and the basis of all human relationships.
Earlier at the start of the Eucharistic celebratiom, Bishop Odoki welcomed pilgrims and guests, thanking God for sustaining participants throughout the Prayer peace Week. He expressed gratitude to the bishop, clergy, and faithful of Lira diocese for their hospitality and appreciated the administration of Lango College, the host venue for providing a conducive environment for the event.
He also thanked all individuals and leaders who contributed towards the success of the function, including government officials and supporters who offered financial and moral support to the bishops’ ministry and the peace initiative.
The bishop while flanked by other bishops of the province concluded by blessing the peace pilgrims, their families, and the nation of Uganda, urging all participants to return home as missionaries of peace and put into practice the knowledge gained during the week-long gathering.
End.

science.title: Regions of low gene expression promote maintenance and adaptation of horizontally acquired genes in yeasts
science.description: We showed previously that yeasts in Starmerella and Wickerhamiella genera (W/S clade) exhibit numbers of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events much larger than found in any other yeast species, with bacteria and other fungi (Pezizomycotina) as donors. Here we shed light on HGT in the W/S clade by carrying out the characterization of xenologous genes present in three species harboring together close to 600 xenologous genes. Metabolic genes were strongly overrepresented and either introduced functions new to yeasts or restored functions that were likely absent in the W/S clade ancestor. RNA-sequencing revealed lower global levels of expression of xenologous vs native yeast genes in two species. This difference is associated with the preferential accumulation of xenologous genes in large, AT-enriched chromosome terminal regions, dubbed “End” domains, characterized by overall lower gene expression. In one species, “End” domains were shown to be more permissive for protein diversification, but only for xenologous genes. We posit that “End” domains may generate favorable conditions for the adaptation and retention of xenologous genes, helping explain the exceptional numbers of HGT events in the W/S clade. Horizontal gene transfer is generally considered uncommon in eukaryotes, but rates are very high in a floral yeast clade. Underlying this may be large, low-expression, chromosomal safe harbors that promote retention and adaptation of incoming genes.
